sections.description: Describes the patient’s presenting symptoms, physical findings and first‑line investigations that raised the suspicion of a systemic inflammatory process with central nervous system involvement.
subtopics: Chief complaints: fever, headache, malaise, hiccups, arthralgia, oral and genital ulcers
Vital signs and initial physical exam findings
Key laboratory abnormalities: hyponatraemia, high CRP, hyper‑CK, hyper‑LFTs, hyper‑glycaemia
Early endocrine assessment confirming SIADH (low serum osmolality, high urine osmolality and sodium, elevated ADH)
Initial imaging (CT head, chest, abdomen) and its normality
Empiric antimicrobial coverage and its rationale

sections.description: Outlines the systematic approach taken to rule out infectious, neoplastic and autoimmune causes before arriving at the diagnosis of concurrent Behçet’s disease and neuro‑Behçet’s disease.
subtopics: CNS infections: viral (HSV, VZV), bacterial, tuberculous meningitis – CSF findings and viral PCR
Primary CNS malignancy: MRI, CSF cytology, sIL‑2R level
Systemic autoimmune disorders: ANA, ANCA, ENA panel, clinical criteria
Neurosarcoidosis: ACE, lysozyme, imaging
Other endocrine or metabolic causes of hyponatraemia
Rationale for limited screening tests and interpretation of non‑specific findings

sections.section_title: 3. Diagnostic Confirmation of Behçet’s Disease and Neuro‑Behçet’s Disease
sections.description: Details how the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease (ICBD) were applied, what mucocutaneous and neurological findings satisfied the criteria, and why neuro‑BD was diagnosed despite normal MRI.
subtopics: ICBD scoring system and patient’s points: oral aphthae, genital ulcers, folliculitis–like rash, fever
Role of HLA‑B51 and its limitations
CSF profile consistent with aseptic meningitis and its significance for neuro‑BD
Normal MRI in early neuro‑BD – pathophysiological explanation and clinical implications
Combined diagnosis of definite BD and acute neuro‑BD

sections.description: Explains the chosen treatment pathway—including colchicine monotherapy and hyponatraemia management—and the evidence (or lack thereof) supporting these choices in acute neuro‑BD.
subtopics: Empiric antimicrobials and antiviral therapy: indications, timing and discontinuation
Colchicine pharmacodynamics: anti‑neutrophilic, anti‑IL‑1β/IL‑6 activity
Evidence base for colchicine in mucocutaneous BD versus neuro‑BD
Fluid restriction for SIADH: monitoring, safety limits, avoidance of rapid correction
Adjunctive wound care: topical steroids, silver sulfadiazine, pain control
Long‑term follow‑up: duration of colchicine, monitoring for recurrence, transition to other therapies

sections.section_title: 5. Outcomes, Clinical Lessons and Prognostic Considerations
sections.description: Reviews the patient’s recovery trajectory, the implications for future practice, and the broader clinical significance of SIADH in acute neuro‑Behçet’s disease.
subtopics: Time course of symptom resolution: fever, neurological deficits, mucocutaneous lesions, hyponatraemia
Normalization of laboratory values: serum sodium, ADH, CK, LFTs
Absence of relapse over four years of colchicine therapy
Potential pathophysiological link between CNS inflammation, IL‑6 and SIADH
Clinical red flags: persistent hiccups, rhabdomyolysis, unexplained hyponatraemia
Recommendations for clinicians: high suspicion for neuro‑BD with concurrent SIADH, choice of therapy when steroids are contraindicated
